841.title: Curse the day (Job 3)
841.hook: Job curses the day he was born, and the Bible keeps every word
841.howItsDone: Jewish tradition has a long practice of lament: the book of Job, Lamentations read on Tisha b'Av, and psalms that question God are all part of the Tanakh and are read and studied aloud.

segments.voice: Yesterday, three friends sat with Job seven days and seven nights, the custom later called shiva. Your line was they said nothing. Today, the silence breaks, and Job is the one who breaks it.

Seven days of quiet, and then: "After this opened Job his mouth, and cursed his day." Two chapters ago, this same man said the LORD gave and the LORD hath taken away, blessed be the name of the LORD. The adversary bet he would curse. Now the first thing out of his mouth is a curse. But the text is precise about the target. Not God. His day, the day he was born. Everything he's held since the messengers came is about to pour out.
screen: `AFTER THIS OPENED JOB HIS MOUTH.` → `HE CURSED HIS DAY.` → `NOT GOD. HIS DAY.`

segments.voice: He begins: "Let the day perish wherein I was born, and the night in which it was said, There is a man child conceived." Erase it from the calendar. "Let that day be darkness; let not God regard it from above, neither let the light shine upon it." Then he goes further, and it's hard to hear: "Why died I not from the womb?" If he'd never lived, he says, he'd be lying still, in the place where the small and the great are together, where the prisoners rest. "There the wicked cease from troubling; and there the weary be at rest." This isn't a man being polite to heaven. It's a cry, the whole chapter of it, and it ends with no answer and no resolution. Notice: this is scripture. The Tanakh didn't cut it, soften it, or add a note telling Job to calm down. His rage sits inside the holy books, read and studied word for word. The Writings also hold Lamentations, and psalms that ask God how long. A tradition that keeps words like these is saying something about what may be said, out loud, in front of God. That doesn't make Job right about everything; the friends will argue with him, and so will God. But the book lets him say it first. If your own grief has ever come out angry, you're in the company of a man the book itself called perfect and upright.
screen: `LET THE DAY PERISH.` · `WHY DIED I NOT FROM THE WOMB?` · `THE WEARY BE AT REST.` · `SCRIPTURE KEEPS EVERY WORD.`

segments.voice: Is there something you're angry about that you've kept polite, a diagnosis, an injustice, a person, a year that went wrong? Say it to yourself in plain words, no softening, not to act on it or to judge the feeling, only to let it be said, the way Job said his. If you pray, you can bring it to God as it is, rough edges and all.
His day. Not God: the day he was born is the target of Job's curse, the one thing he wants erased. Today's word.
Your line: rage is allowed. Saying it isn't the same as acting on it. See you tomorrow.

842.title: Don't explain their pain (Job 4–5)
842.hook: the friends insist the innocent never suffer
842.carry: the book won't let it fit
842.tomorrow: I would speak to the Almighty
842.howItsDone: Jewish teaching on comforting mourners, drawn partly from Job's friends, warns against explaining a death or a loss to the bereaved; visitors are encouraged to listen and let the mourner lead.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Job broke seven days of silence by cursing the day he was born. Your line was rage is allowed. Today, his friend answers him.

"Everything happens for a reason." It gets said at hospital bedsides and after funerals, by kind people who want to help. Eliphaz, the first friend to speak, is that kind of person. He starts gently, almost apologizing: "If we assay to commune with thee, wilt thou be grieved? but who can withhold himself from speaking?" In plain words: I know this might hurt, but I can't keep quiet. He reminds Job that he's comforted others, strengthened weak hands, steadied stumbling knees. Now it's come to you, he says, and you're shaken. Then he asks his real question.
screen: `EVERYTHING HAPPENS FOR A REASON.` → `ELIPHAZ SPEAKS FIRST.` → `WHO CAN KEEP FROM SPEAKING?`

segments.voice: "Remember, I pray thee, who ever perished, being innocent? or where were the righteous cut off?" Name one innocent person who was ever destroyed. You can't. Think what that means, Job. He backs it with what he's seen: "they that plow iniquity, and sow wickedness, reap the same." He even describes a vision in the night, a spirit gliding past his face, his hair standing up, a whisper asking whether any mortal can be more just than God. By chapter five he offers hope on the same terms: "Behold, happy is the man whom God correcteth." Take the correction, and you'll be restored. Much of this sounds like wisdom you could hear anywhere: good things grow from good seeds; God is greater than we are. But he's saying it to a man in ashes, scraping his skin, whose children are dead. Aimed at him, every general truth becomes an accusation: you must have done something. And we know what Eliphaz doesn't. Chapter one told us Job is perfect and upright, and his suffering began with a question asked in heaven, not with anything he did. Eliphaz has a theory that explains the world, and he needs Job's suffering to fit it. The book won't let it fit. At the very end, God will say the friends haven't spoken rightly. Notice how the explaining starts: kindly, reasonably, from a friend who sat in silence for seven days.

segments.voice: Remember a time someone explained your pain to you, maybe kindly, it was meant to be, at least you have, God doesn't give you more than you can handle, and notice how it landed; then, with no shame, a time you did it to someone else. Think of one person hurting now, and try what you might say instead: I'm here, I'm so sorry, tell me. If you pray, you can pray for them without trying to make sense of it.

843.title: I would speak to the Almighty (Job 13:3)
843.word: I would speak to the Almighty
843.hook: Job demands a hearing with God
843.carry: I would speak to the almighty
843.howItsDone: Jewish tradition includes prayer that questions and argues with God, from Abraham at Sodom and Moses after the golden calf to Job, and these texts are read and studied as part of the Tanakh.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Eliphaz asked who ever perished, being innocent. Your line was the book won't let it fit. Today, Job has heard enough explaining.

By chapter thirteen, each of the friends has had a turn to explain, and Job has had it with them. "Ye are forgers of lies," he tells them, "ye are all physicians of no value." Doctors who can't heal. Then a line that's almost funny, if it weren't so tired: "O that ye would altogether hold your peace! and it should be your wisdom." If you'd just stay quiet, that would be your wisdom. It's hard not to hear the seven silent days behind it. Then he turns away from them entirely, because the friends aren't the ones he needs to talk to.
screen: `PHYSICIANS OF NO VALUE.` → `HOLD YOUR PEACE.` → `JOB TURNS AWAY FROM THEM.`

segments.voice: "Surely I would speak to the Almighty, and I desire to reason with God." The friends have been talking about God. Job wants to talk to God. Not a lecture, not a guess: a hearing, face to face. It sounds like a courtroom: "Behold now, I have ordered my cause; I know that I shall be justified." He has prepared his case, and he'll argue it. In the middle of the defiance comes a line people quote in very different moods: "Though he slay me, yet will I trust in him: but I will maintain mine own ways before him." Trust and argument in one breath. Job doesn't stop believing God is there. That's exactly why he won't stop talking: you only demand a hearing from someone you think is listening. It's an old thread in the Tanakh. Abraham, hearing that Sodom will be destroyed, asks God, "Shall not the Judge of all the earth do right?" Moses argues for his people after the golden calf. Jewish tradition has room for prayer that pushes back, that brings a complaint, that says this isn't fair, to God's face. Job isn't asking his friends to let him off. He's asking God to show up. That's a kind of faith too, the kind that won't go quiet.
screen: `NOT ABOUT GOD. TO GOD.` · `I HAVE ORDERED MY CAUSE.` · `THOUGH HE SLAY ME, YET WILL I TRUST.` · `ABRAHAM ARGUED TOO.`

segments.voice: Is something in your life not fair, not someone else's case, but yours? Say it inside in one or two plain sentences, the way you'd lay out facts to a judge: this happened, this is what it cost, this is what I don't understand. If you pray, you can say it to God as plainly as Job did; if not, say it to the quiet and hear yourself say it.
I would speak to the Almighty. Job turns from his friends and asks for a hearing with God, to argue his case face to face. Today's word.

844.title: My redeemer liveth (Job 19:25)
844.hook: a flash of hope in the middle of despair
844.howItsDone: Jewish readers study Job 19:25 alongside the go'el, the redeeming kinsman of the Torah and the book of Ruth, and God is called redeemer, go'el, in the Tanakh and in daily Jewish prayer.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Job turned from his friends and asked for a hearing with God. Your line was I would speak to the almighty. Today, in the middle of that argument, a light comes on.

Chapter nineteen finds Job very low. His brothers are far from him, his friends have forgotten him, his servants treat him like a stranger, and his breath is strange to his own wife. He begs, in the old Jewish Publication Society translation: "Have pity upon me, have pity upon me, O ye my friends; for the hand of God hath touched me." Then a wish: "Oh that my words were now written! Oh that they were inscribed in a book! That with an iron pen and lead they were graven in the rock for ever!" Carve it in stone, so somebody, someday, knows what happened to me.
screen: `FORGOTTEN BY FRIENDS.` → `HAVE PITY UPON ME.` → `CARVE MY WORDS IN THE ROCK.`

segments.voice: Then, suddenly: "But as for me, I know that my Redeemer liveth, and that He will witness at the last upon the dust." From the bottom of the pit, I know. The Hebrew for redeemer is go'el, and it runs through the book of Ruth too: Boaz was the go'el, the kinsman with the right and duty to buy back a family's land and keep a dead man's name alive. In the Torah, a go'el is the relative who buys back what you lost. So Job, forgotten by everyone, says someone will stand up for me. The text doesn't say who, and readers hear it more than one way. Some hear God himself, the God Job is arguing with, somehow also his defender. Some connect it to a line a few chapters earlier, "my Witness is in heaven," and hear a defender on Job's side in the heavenly court. Christians read this verse too, and hear it about Jesus. The lines right after it are hard Hebrew, and translations differ. But the first half stands clear. And notice where it comes: not after his health returns, not after an answer, but in the middle of being forgotten. Hope here isn't the end of the pain. It's a flash inside it. And Job's wish came true in its own way: his words were written in a book, and people still read them.
screen: `MY REDEEMER LIVETH.` · `GO'EL: THE KINSMAN WHO BUYS BACK.` · `GOD, OR A WITNESS IN HEAVEN?` · `HOPE INSIDE THE PAIN.`

segments.voice: If something feels heavy right now, let it be there, and inside it look for one small hope: someone who will stand up for you, a morning you're looking forward to, a belief that holds you. Hold it the way Job held his, not instead of the hard thing but right in the middle of it. If you pray, you can say Job's line, I know that my redeemer liveth.
Go'el. Forgotten by his friends, Job says there is a go'el, a redeemer who will stand up for him, alive. Today's word.
Your line: a flash inside it. Job said I know before anything got better. Until tomorrow.

845.title: Where is wisdom? (Job 28)
845.hook: miners dig out gold, "But wisdom, where shall it be found?"
845.howItsDone: Job 28 is studied in Jewish tradition as a poem on wisdom, and its closing line, the fear of the Lord is wisdom, echoes a teaching found also in Psalms and Proverbs.

segments.voice: Yesterday, from the bottom of the pit, Job said I know that my redeemer liveth. Your line was a flash inside it. Today, the arguing stops for a while, and the book goes underground.

"Surely there is a vein for the silver, and a place for gold where they fine it." Chapter twenty-eight opens in a mine. Someone cuts a shaft far from where people live and hangs on ropes, swinging, forgotten by anyone walking above. They turn the mountains over by the roots, cut channels in the rock, find sapphires in the stones and dust of gold. They go where no bird has gone: "There is a path which no fowl knoweth, and which the vulture's eye hath not seen." Down in the dark, they bring hidden things into the light. Human beings, the poem says, can find almost anything.
screen: `A VEIN FOR THE SILVER.` → `HANGING ON ROPES IN THE DARK.` → `A PATH NO BIRD KNOWS.`

segments.voice: Almost. Then the turn: "But where shall wisdom be found? and where is the place of understanding?" We can dig to the roots of mountains, but nobody knows the way to that. "The depth saith, It is not in me: and the sea saith, It is not with me." Can you buy it? The poem runs through the treasure room: gold, onyx, sapphire, coral, pearls, rubies, the topaz of Ethiopia. None of it is enough. Then where? "God understandeth the way thereof, and he knoweth the place thereof." And the chapter ends with what God says to human beings: "Behold, the fear of the Lord, that is wisdom; and to depart from evil is understanding." Notice where this poem sits. Job and his friends have argued chapter after chapter, the friends sure they know why Job suffers, Job sure they're wrong. Then this quiet poem drops in, like a pause in a shouting match. Readers debate who is speaking: some hear Job, some hear the narrator stepping in. Either way, it tells everyone at the table: you can mine the earth, but you can't mine this. Wisdom here isn't a pile of answers; the friends had answers. It's a way of standing, in awe of God and turned away from harm. It's what's left when the explanations run out.
screen: `WHERE SHALL WISDOM BE FOUND?` · `THE DEPTH SAITH, IT IS NOT IN ME.` · `NOT FOR GOLD OR RUBIES.` · `GOD UNDERSTANDETH THE WAY THEREOF.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one question you've been digging at, why did this happen, what should I have done, and notice how hard you've been digging. Then set the shovel down and ask a different question: how do I want to stand while I don't know, gently, honestly, turned away from harm? If you pray, you can bring the question to God and leave it there for now.

846.title: Out of the whirlwind (Job 38–39)
846.hook: God answers with stars, sea and wild goats: "Where wast thou?", and no explanation
846.howItsDone: Jews read God's speeches from the whirlwind near the end of the book of Job, and Jewish readers have understood them in more than one way, as rebuke, as comfort, and as an answer that is God's presence rather than an explanation.

segments.voice: Yesterday, a poem went down into the mines and asked where wisdom could be found. Your line was where shall wisdom be found. Today, Job finally gets the hearing he asked for.

Chapter after chapter, Job has demanded it: let God come, let me lay out my case. And the friends have answered for God, again and again. Then, after all of it: "Then the LORD answered Job out of the whirlwind, and said." A voice out of the storm. Job has his speech ready. The reader has questions too: will God mention the adversary, the test, the children, the boils? Will God explain? And the first thing God does is ask a question back.
screen: `JOB DEMANDED A HEARING.` → `A VOICE OUT OF THE STORM.` → `WILL GOD EXPLAIN?`

segments.voice: "Where wast thou when I laid the foundations of the earth? declare, if thou hast understanding." Then the questions keep coming. Who measured the earth, stretched the line on it, laid its cornerstone, "When the morning stars sang together, and all the sons of God shouted for joy?" Who shut in the sea with doors, and told it, "Hitherto shalt thou come, but no further: and here shall thy proud waves be stayed"? Have you walked the springs of the sea, or seen the storehouses of the snow? Can you bind the Pleiades, or loosen the bands of Orion? Then the animals: the lioness hunting for her cubs, the raven's young crying for food. "Knowest thou the time when the wild goats of the rock bring forth?" The wild donkey that laughs at the city, the ostrich, the horse, the hawk. And God sends rain "on the wilderness, wherein there is no man." Rain no human will ever see. Here's what God never says: nothing about the adversary or the test, no reason for the boils or the house that fell. Job asked why, and God answered with the universe. Some readers hear a rebuke: who are you to question me? Some hear a strange comfort: the world is far bigger than Job's pain, and God cares for corners no human has visited, wild goats giving birth on a cliff with no one watching. Both readings agree on one thing. Job asked for a hearing, and God came.
screen: `WHERE WAST THOU?` · `WHEN THE MORNING STARS SANG.` · `WILD GOATS, AND RAIN WHERE NO MAN IS.` · `NO EXPLANATION. GOD CAME.`

segments.voice: Find something you didn't make, the sky through a window, a tree, a bird, a weed in a crack, or if you can't move, picture the night sky. Let the whirlwind's questions come, where was I when this was made, who waters this, and let your own worries stand next to something much larger. If you pray, you can simply look, and let the looking be your prayer.

847.title: Job spoke right (Job 42:7–17)
847.hook: God says the friends were wrong and Job was right; Job prays for them
847.carry: the man who cried out was right
847.howItsDone: Job belongs to the Writings, the third part of the Tanakh. Jews read and study it as a book that argues with God about suffering, and some readers take its last chapter as a model of praying for those who wronged you.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the voice out of the whirlwind asked Job about the Pleiades, the sea and wild goats. Your line was where wast thou. Today, the last chapter of Job, and the end of the week.

Three friends sat with Job in the dust, then argued with him for a long stretch of the book. You must have done something, they said. God is just, so your suffering has a reason. Confess, and it will get better. Job refused. He cursed the day he was born, demanded a hearing, called out to God. Then God spoke from the whirlwind, and Job went quiet. A reader might expect the verdict to fall on Job. It falls somewhere else.
screen: `THREE FRIENDS WITH ANSWERS.` → `JOB REFUSES THEIR ANSWERS.` → `THE VERDICT FALLS ELSEWHERE.`

segments.voice: God turns, not to Job, but to Eliphaz. In the King James words: "My wrath is kindled against thee, and against thy two friends: for ye have not spoken of me the thing that is right, as my servant Job hath." The friends defended God and said all the careful, tidy things, and God says they were wrong. Job accused, protested, wept and asked why, and God calls him my servant and says he spoke right. Readers still puzzle over what Job got right. Some say his honesty: he wouldn't pretend his suffering made sense. Others say he spoke to God, while his friends only spoke about God. The text doesn't settle it, and this path won't either. Then a second turn. The friends must bring an offering, and Job, the man they lectured, is to pray for them. And the LORD turned the captivity of Job when he prayed for his friends. His restoring begins there, in a prayer for the people who hurt him. His family and old acquaintances come to eat bread with him and comfort him. He is given twice as much as he had before. He has daughters again, and the text names them, Jemima, Keziah and Keren-happuch, and says their father gave them an inheritance among their brothers. Some readers find this ending too neat; others hear a gift that never erases what was lost. Either way, the book ends with Job old and full of days.
screen: `GOD TURNS TO THE FRIENDS.` · then, large: `YE HAVE NOT SPOKEN OF ME THE THING THAT IS RIGHT.` · `JOB PRAYS FOR THOSE WHO LECTURED HIM.` · then: `THE DAUGHTERS ARE NAMED.`

segments.voice: This week in Job ran from a cursed day, through friends explaining pain, a man asking to speak to the Almighty, a redeemer who lives and wisdom that can't be bought, to a whirlwind. Now bring to mind someone ordinary who hurt you, maybe with words meant to help, and say their name once, inside. If you pray, pray for them in your own words or your tradition's; if not, simply wish them one good thing.
My servant. God calls Job, not the friends with neat answers, my servant, and says he spoke right. Today's word.
Your line: the man who cried out was right. His restoring began with a prayer for his friends. Day eight hundred forty-seven, done.
